prompt: You're given an array of integers sorted in ascending order and a target. Return the positions of two numbers that add up to the target, using only constant extra space.
why: Sorted + a pair + O(1) space: start at both ends. Sum too small → move left in; too big → move right in.
trap: A hashmap solves the unsorted version but breaks the space limit. Binary search per element works but is O(n log n).

prompt: Decide whether a sentence reads the same forwards and backwards once you ignore punctuation, spaces and letter case.
tells: reads the same forwards and backwards
why: Compare mirrored positions: one pointer from each end, moving inward and skipping non-letters.
trap: There's no window to maintain. You're comparing the two ends, not tracking a range.

prompt: Vertical walls of different heights stand at equal spacing along a line. Pick two walls so that the water held between them is as large as possible.
why: Start with the widest pair. The shorter wall caps the area, so moving it inward is the only move that can help.
trap: Grabbing the two tallest walls (heap) ignores the width between them.

prompt: Find every distinct triple of numbers in an unsorted array whose sum is zero. The answer must not contain duplicate triples.
why: Sort first, fix one number, then run two inward pointers over the rest: O(n²). Sorting also makes skipping duplicates easy.
trap: “Unsorted” scares people off. You are allowed to sort it yourself, and n ≤ 3000 says O(n²) is fine.

prompt: An array holds only the values 0, 1 and 2. Rearrange it in place so all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s, in a single pass.
why: Three pointers (low, mid, high) partition the array in one sweep: swap 0s back, 2s forward.
trap: Counting each value then rewriting works, but it takes two passes.

prompt: Two sorted arrays are given; the first has enough empty slots at its end to hold the second. Merge them into the first array without allocating a new one.
why: Walk both arrays from the back, writing the larger value into the last free slot.
trap: A heap merges k lists. With only two, one pointer per array is enough.

prompt: Given a sorted list, remove repeated values in place so each value appears once, and return the new length. Elements past that length don't matter.
why: A slow pointer marks where to write; a fast pointer scans for the next new value.
trap: Looks like a window, but no range property is being maintained. It's a read head and a write head.

prompt: Given a sorted array that may contain negative numbers, return the square of each value, also in sorted order, in linear time.
why: The biggest squares sit at the two ends. Compare the ends and fill the output from the back.
trap: Square-then-sort is O(n log n). “Linear time” rules it out.

prompt: Given two strings s and t, decide whether s can be formed by deleting some characters of t without reordering the rest.
why: One pointer in each string; advance in s only on a match. Reaching the end of s means yes. O(n), O(1) space.
trap: Subsequence questions often need DP, but a single yes/no check against one string just needs two pointers.

prompt: Each boat carries at most two people with total weight at most a limit. Given everyone's weight, sorted, find the fewest boats needed.
why: Pair the heaviest remaining person with the lightest if they fit; walk the two ends inward.
trap: It feels greedy, and it is, but the mechanics are two pointers on a sorted array.

prompt: Find three numbers in an array whose sum is closest to a target. Return that sum.
why: Sort, fix one number, then move two pointers inward on the rest while tracking the best sum. O(n²).
trap: Trying every triple by backtracking is O(n³); sorting unlocks the two-pointer squeeze.
